1:
What the second vision is for they agree on, and one measures it out. Gill calls it another vision, like the first in some things and different in others, serving partly to represent the burning of the city and partly the Lord's removal. Keil and Delitzsch divide the chapter on exactly that line, the first eight verses showing how the city is to be burned and the rest how Jehovah will forsake his temple. Calvin states the design before touching the words: God meant to bear witness that he had nothing further in common with them, and set his majesty before them so fearfully that the threat might strike the obstinate. Clarke reads the removal as gradual, the divine presence withdrawing farther and farther from the temple.

Why the living creatures are now called cherubim Ellicott settles in a line: the one word answers throughout to the other. Calvin explains the change instead: the first vision came by a river in a profane country, when the exiles were far from the temple, and now that the scene is the temple God begins to speak familiarly and explain what had been too obscure. Clarke stands back from the whole apparatus: the prophet several times calls his vision a similitude of the glory of Jehovah, which is to say a set of hieroglyphics by which that glory was in some measure represented.

Henry takes the throne devotionally and warns about the medium: here is something of the invisible world set out in the visible, faint representations and shadows, no more to be compared with the truth than a picture with the life, yet enough to oblige us to the utmost reverence. God is above the cherubim in respect not of dignity only but of dominion, since they have great power and wisdom and are all subject; and the firmament is one of his prospect as well as of his power, for from it he beholds the children of men.

Who the man in linen is divides them. Ellicott and Calvin agree that he is the same person as before and that the change of office is the point: he had been employed in mercy and protection, and now the same agent executes judgment, as love turns to wrath by impenitence and blessings become curses by abuse. Calvin puts it as the standing double office of angels, ministers of favour toward the faithful who at the same command execute vengeance. Gill takes him for no angel at all, but a figure of the invading army.

The coals and the burning they date differently. Clarke makes them signify the burning by the Chaldeans, and observes that the space between the four wheels was all on fire, the coals taken from there. Gill says the man represents the Chaldean or the Roman army, and holds the vision to refer chiefly if not altogether to the later destruction. Ellicott stays with what the coals mean rather than when: taken from between the cherubim, they signify in every possible way that the doom is not from man's will, however men are used as instruments, nor from any accident, but from God himself.

Two smaller points, and a clash of method on one of them. Gill takes the cherubim's standing on the right for the south side, farthest from the northern idolatries, so that they bear testimony against them; Calvin forbids the exercise, since we are not to seek cunning speculations about the right hand, the detail serving only to show the way open and the vision certain, that no suspicion might creep in of an empty spectre. On the departure, Ellicott notes the singular cherub for the usual plural, and marks the striking contrast with the dedication, when the same cloud filled the house as God came; Clarke marks the similarity instead. Calvin says plainly that the temple was stripped of its furniture: without God what remained?
5:
What the sound of the wings is they take three ways. Ellicott hears machinery: the noise shows the cherubim already in motion, since when they stood they let their wings down, so that they were on the eve of departure and the movement great enough to carry to the outer court. Clarke and Calvin hear thunder, which was called the voice of God; Calvin adds that no concussion could be more severe, and that the sound marks a change both unusual and incomprehensible. Gill hears the Gospel: a joyful sound of grace and mercy, of life, liberty, pardon and salvation, carried into all the earth by the swift ministry of the apostles, of which the wings are the sign, until the whole world was filled with the brightness of the glory.

Ellicott alone works out the order of the narrative, and denies that it is chronological. The two verses about the coals are not later in time than the sound of the wings but a more particular account, given parenthetically, of what had been mentioned briefly before; and the long description that follows is largely a repetition of the first vision, supplied in pieces as the narrative advances rather than in sequence. He also observes, in passing, that the plural ending added to cherubim throughout the chapter is unnecessary, the word being already plural in Hebrew.

Calvin makes the errand a demolition of confidence. The Jews thought themselves always safe, and that the sacred fire on the altar availed to expiate all wickedness; God shows instead that he so resided in the temple as to clothe himself with wrath against them, the cherubim keeping the very arms by which they were at last to be destroyed. The false and perverse glorying that had intoxicated them, that God was in some way bound to them exclusively, is cut away from under them. He reads the wings the same way, as a mark of subordination: they signify that angels have no proper or independent motion but are governed by a secret instinct, which is why they are winged in the sanctuary too.

The hand under the wings sets Clarke reconstructing. He holds still that hands and wings were not distinct: the arms were feathered like wings and the hand ended the arm, but the long front feathers reached well beyond the fingers, so that the hands would appear to be underneath. And he draws a moral from the shape of the member, that a human hand may signify how God helps and punishes man by man, using human agency in the general operations of his providence. Gill keeps to the action, one of the four putting out his hand from among the rest. Henry looks past the machinery to the omen it introduces, the departure of the glory that would open the door for ruin to break in, so that those who had provoked God to go might know what they had lost and lament after him, groaning out their Ichabod.
9:
Two allegories are laid over the same machinery. Gill reads it ecclesiologically: the wheels are the churches and the cherubim their ministers, the four sides mark the uniformity of Gospel churches in every condition, the likeness of body and wings the agreement of ministers in doctrine and work, and the wheels go beside the cherubim because ministers are guides to churches. Calvin and Wesley read the same parts providentially. Wheels are the fittest image of change, Calvin says, since nothing in the world is stationary and revolutions are continually happening; and because affairs are so tumultuous, profane men cannot see that the world is governed by a fixed counsel and fabricate a blind fortune, so that God in concession to our weakness draws all events under the figure of a wheel.

The eyes are where that reading pays. Calvin makes events full of eyes because they hang on secret commands, wheels being properly without sense, so that God's voice is heard by every creature and no motion happens apart from that instinct. Wesley puts it in one sentence: events are not determined by the wheel of fortune, which is blind, but by the wheels of providence, which are full of eyes; and adds that their motions look intricate to us, even contrary, while all tend jointly to one end. Calvin guards against a false inference: the one likeness does not mean God governs equably, which experience contradicts, but that the variety darkening our eyes does not disturb the tenor of his works.

Clarke rejects the usual mechanics. A wheel within a wheel is generally taken as one cutting another at right angles, but that will not account for the motions attributed to them, and he cannot see how they could move at all on that supposition, since if one turned on its axis the other must be dragged across its own; he conjectures a wheel with two rims on a single axis, adding that it is no matter of faith and the reader may judge as he will. On the stone he is as careful: the versions give chrysolith, jacinth and carbuncle for one word, the beryl runs from green into blue and yellow while the ancients' chrysolith was our topaz, and one name served for several gems of nearly the same colour, where the moderns go by chemical characters. Wesley says only, sea-green.

The cry to the wheels produces the sharpest thing here. Clarke calls the received rendering the most unfortunate and unmeaning translation ever made, since the word may mean the roller, a chariot, or roll on; and he turns on a preacher who took the exclamation for a text and extracted the decree of eternal predestination from it, saying such working of God's word cannot be too severely reprehended. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same by grammar: the rendering that makes it a name given to the wheels leaves the words in my hearing an unmeaning addition, whereas the verb means addressing, so that the wheels were called on to whirl and verify their name. Wesley keeps only that one guided them, as by vocal direction.

The face of a cherub sets two working backwards. Clarke observes that the same face is called the face of an ox in the first vision, and infers that a cherub was in the likeness of an ox, at least as to the head; the word never occurs as a verb, so its meaning cannot be precisely fixed, and he reports a lexicographer who reads the first letter as a note of similitude, gets like the mighty one from it, and makes the cherubim an emblem of the Trinity. Calvin notices the other change, cherubim under a form unlike the pair in the sanctuary, and explains four against two by the grossness of a people that made it necessary to bend aside from the first institution.
18:
Ellicott alone traces the departure as a sequence of stations: the cherubim had stood by the right side of the house, then the glory left the threshold and resumed its place above them where they waited, and now the whole rises from the earth and moves to the east gate, which is the main entrance of the outermost court. Gill counts it another step towards a general departure and another signal given; Wesley names that gate the court of the people. Calvin puts the principal point plainly, that God had deserted the temple.

What made the desertion unthinkable to them Calvin sets out. On the strength of the promise that the temple should be the place of his rest they did not think it possible that God would ever leave, so they sinned without restraint; and while they drove him far off by their crimes they still wished to have him bound to them in some way. The folly had been derided already by the earlier prophet who asked, with heaven for a seat and earth for a footstool, what house men proposed to build.

One word divides the two shortest comments. Ellicott says that every one is not in the original and should be struck out, since they stood, or it stood, would be better and the vision is to be taken as a whole. Wesley builds his best sentence on the words Ellicott would delete: the glory, the cherubim and the wheels all stood, respiting execution and giving opportunity of preventing the approaching misery.

Clarke objects to the plural and then makes an admission. Hebrew masculine nouns end in the plural as this one does, so the English s should never have been added and ought to be uniformly expunged, the singular being cherub and the plural cherubim. Then, at the close of the chapter, he says he has met with nothing on the subject that entirely satisfies himself, having tried only to make the literal meaning plain; and he adds why he stops there, that he does not like conjectures on divine things, since many points which had no other origin are now incorporated with creeds that it is deemed sinful to doubt.

Why the vision is repeated at all they answer three ways. Gill takes the repetition as carrying an addition, that the figure on the throne is the God of Israel, and argues from it, since the Father never appeared in human form, that Christ is meant and the deity of Christ thereby proved. Calvin makes the second showing a confirmation, not for one man's private advantage, since the prophet was persuaded already, but for the people, or at least to leave without excuse those who despised a favour so manifest; and he explains the further repetitions inside the chapter by the temper of the hearers, a people dull and slow who added to their other faults an open endeavour to detract from the authority of every prophet, so that what was clear enough had to be inculcated again. Wesley asks instead how the prophet knew the creatures, and allows two answers, special assurance or comparison with what he had often seen in the temple.
